The analysis above suggests that the core problem is not the absence of law, but the absence of sufficiently tailored law. Existing international and domestic frameworks already reach orbital data centers in important ways, but they do so unevenly.
What is needed now is more coherent coverage.

It is already visible in pilot deployments, formal FCC filings, public moonshot projects, and active commercialization efforts. The recommendations that follow are designed to close those gaps without requiring an entirely new legal architecture. They call for clearer national authorization, stronger international standards, continuity between terrestrial and orbital AI and data regulation, greater transparency, investment in risk-reducing technologies, and early attention to competition and equitable access.
First, spacefaring states should build clear authorization pathways for on-orbit activities not squarely captured by older launch, spectrum, or remote-sensing frameworks.

Third, AI and data governance regimes should expressly reject the notion that space creates a regulatory safe harbor. The EU AI Act’s scope already provides a useful example by reaching certain third country providers and deployers when their systems are placed on the market in the Union or their outputs are used in the Union. A similar continuity principle should guide privacy, cybersecurity, consumer-protection, and AI-safety regulation elsewhere: orbital processing should not alter the substantive responsibilities of providers merely because the hardware sits above the atmosphere. Fourth, regulators and operators should place much greater emphasis on transparency and confidence-building. Registration data, conjunction statistics, disposal performance, major cyber incidents, and basic mission-purpose disclosures are all likely to matter more as orbital AI infrastructure scales.Fifth, law should encourage protective technologies rather than merely punish failure. Cyber hardening, authenticated software updates, strong encryption, on-orbit servicing, active debris removal, and collision-avoidance systems all reduce legal as well as operational risk. Finally, policymakers should begin thinking now about concentration and access. If orbital compute becomes a meaningful layer of global digital infrastructure, competition, interoperability, and equitable access will become legal questions, not merely market outcomes.

If policymakers move early, orbital AI infrastructure may develop within a framework that protects safety, preserves access, clarifies jurisdiction, and reduces the risks that orbit becomes either a regulatory lawless data haven or an unusable debris field. If they move too slowly, the law will again be left catching up after technical and commercial realities have already hardened.

For that reason, the governance of orbital AI infrastructure may become one of the clearest tests of whether 20th century space law can be made equal to 21st century digital infrastructure. The new space race has already begun. The question is not whether space-based infrastructure will continue to expand—it already is—but whether the law will be ready when it does.

Even if orbital data centers never achieve commercial viability at scale, the broader point remains. The volume of satellites and space-based infrastructure now entering low-Earth orbit— communications mega-constellations, Earth-observation networks, in-orbit servicing vehicles, and experimental computing nodes—already far exceeds what was contemplated when the five foundational treaties of international space law were negotiated. Those instruments were drafted for an era of state-led missions numbering in the dozens, not privately operated constellations numbering in the tens of thousands. Whether or not orbital data centers become the next major infrastructure class, the legal architecture governing space must evolve to address the density, diversity, and commercial character of twenty-first century orbital activity. Orbital data centers simply make that imperative harder to ignore.
